newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices rise with futures market - NYT.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices rise with futures market - NYT.

text.p: Perculating prices of coffee in the futures trading pit have been spilling over into the retail arena, making it more expensive to get a good cup of java across the U.S., the New York Times said.
In Tuesday's editions, the Times said that the increase in retail prices is caused in part by the increased popularity of good coffee and shortages in stockpiles.
In the past four months, there has been an uninterrupted run-up in the price of coffee, leading to the longest sustained price rise in 20 years.
That surge has been trickling down to the customer.

Allon Azulai, the owner of Ozzie's Coffee with shops in Brooklyn, said he has raised the price of a cup of coffee by a dime and a pound of beans by $0.50, his first increase in three years of operation.

"When I first opened, I was paying less than $4 for a pound of really good coffee," Azulai said, referring to wholesale costs. "Now it's up to $6 a pound. If the futures market hits $3, I'll have to pay $8 a pound for roasted regular. You add another dollar for decaf, and a dollar for flavor, and its 10 bucks a pound -- wholesale."
In March, Starbucks Corp increased prices by $0.05 for each beverage and $0.30 a pound of beans. It has not ruled out future increases, the Times said.
Makers of canned coffee also have raised prices.

Procter & Gamble Co's Folgers has risen $0.80 to $3.06 since March for a 13-ounce can; Maxwell House, a product of Philip Morris Cos Inc's Kraft General Foods unit, now costs $2.86 a can, a rise of $0.60. Eight O'Clock coffee, the brand of coffee put out by A&P Supermarkets is up $0.20 to $3.26 for 13 ounces.
